I've traced the interactions wiring and component registry model. Here's what the smallest JS behavior pattern looks like, how custom-components fits, and the architectural boundaries.

---

## Smallest Existing JS Behavior Pattern

**`close-button`** is the minimal template:

- **Behavior** (`initCloseButton`): [formats/interactions/src/behaviors/close-button.ts](formats/interactions/src/behaviors/close-button.ts#L14-L43) — Pure function, 30 lines. Accepts `btn: HTMLElement`, wires one `click` listener, returns nothing (no cleanup needed).

- **Vite build**: [formats/interactions/vite.config.ts](formats/interactions/vite.config.ts#L1-L56) — Entry points auto-discovered in `src/components/*.ts`, each becomes `dist/{name}.mjs` + IIFE via `build-iife.ts`.

## Complexity Step Up: Tab Selection Behavior

For anything that needs state management or cleanup:

- **Behavior** (`initTabs`): [formats/interactions/src/behaviors/tabs.ts](formats/interactions/src/behaviors/tabs.ts#L7-L60) — Manages multi-tab selection, keyboard navigation (arrow, Home, End), returns `{ cleanup(): void }`.

- **Web component usage**: [renderers/web-components/src/elements/tabs.ts](renderers/web-components/src/elements/tabs.ts#L37-L46) — Calls `initTabs()` in `connectedCallback()`, stores handle, calls `cleanup()` in `disconnectedCallback()`.

---

## Architecture Boundary: Custom-Components vs Interactions

**Key distinction:**

| Package | Role | Can export JS? | Current Exports |
|---------|------|---|---|
| `@pantoken/plugin-custom-components` | CSS-only layouts (card, banner, button-set) | **Registry model is CSS-only** — see [plugins/pantoken/custom-components/package.json](plugins/pantoken/custom-components/package.json#L18-L27) exports (only `.css` + `.mjs` plugin entry) | CSS rules via `cardRules()`, `bannerRules()`, etc. |
| `@pantoken/interactions` | JS behaviors + IIFE bundles | **Yes, by design** — [formats/interactions/package.json](formats/interactions/package.json#L20-L26) exports individual component entries + full index | `initCloseButton`, `initTabs`, etc. + 30+ per-component IIFE bundles |

> 1. **Extend custom-components to export behaviors** — Add a second export (not the plugin, but direct behavior functions) alongside the CSS. Builds as `segmented-control.mjs`, skeleton-loader.mjs` from [plugins/pantoken/custom-components/vite.config.ts](plugins/pantoken/custom-components/vite.config.ts#L24-L31) pack entry.
> 
> 2. **Keep custom-components CSS-only; add behaviors to `@pantoken/interactions`** — Follow interactions' pattern: add `initSegmentedControl()` and `initSkeletonLoader()` behaviors, autogenerate IIFE entry points via [formats/interactions/scripts/generate-components.ts](formats/interactions/scripts/generate-components.ts), add to [formats/interactions/vite.config.ts#L8-L35](formats/interactions/vite.config.ts#L8-L35) `ALL_COMPONENTS` list.

- [renderers/web-components/package.json](renderers/web-components/package.json#L19-L30) exports `.mjs` entries alongside CSS — same pattern could work for custom-components.

**Evidence for Path 2 (interactions owns behaviors):**
- [formats/interactions/README.md](formats/interactions/README.md#L1-L40) establishes interactions as the sole behavior layer.
- [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#L157-L165) lists interactions as owner of "shared behavior extraction for components."
- Web components use interactions exclusively: [renderers/web-components/src/elements](renderers/web-components/src/elements) imports from `@pantoken/interactions`, never custom-components.

**If Path 1 (custom-components exports JS):**

- **styleItem** (current custom-components pattern): [docs/scripts/registry-plugins.ts](docs/scripts/registry-plugins.ts#L33-L68) — CSS-only, entry = `{ name, category, description, styles: [{ name, path, url }] }`. No JS wiring.

**Interactions test structure:**

- Test file: `tests/<behavior-name>.test.ts`
- Environment: `@vitest-environment happy-dom` (lightweight DOM simulator)
- Pattern: Import `init<Behavior>()`, manually set up HTML, call function, assert DOM mutations

* SkeletonLoader provides animated placeholder content that indicates where data will appear while a page or section is loading. Available in Text, Avatar, and Image types with configurable size (xxs–xxl) and a row slot for additional lines. * SkeletonLoader itself renders exactly one shape (1). Extra lines come from a separate slot (2). Every visible shape and row shares the same shimmer layer (3). The loading semantics — isLoading, aria-busy, the SR-only status announcement — live one level up, in a container you compose yourself (4), not inside SkeletonLoader. 1 — Shape: The type variant: a Text bar, Avatar, or Image block. This is the only part SkeletonLoader itself renders. 2 — Row slot: Swap one or more .skeletonRow instances into the row slot. Shown here: 3 rows. 3 — Shimmer sweep: The .animation gradient overlay inside every shape and row. Sweeps left-to-right in sync across everything visible. See Behaviour. Variants Property table SkeletonLoader exposes Type (Text, Avatar, Image) and Size (xxs–xxl on Text; md only on Avatar/Image). Additional lines are composed through the row slot — swap in one or more .skeletonRow instances, or set hasSlot to false to render a single shape with no slot content. Sizing Size applies to Text only. Each step sets the bar to the font-size of the text it stands in for (bar = 1 × fs). The bar sits inside a row with 0.125 × fs padding above and below, so each row totals 1.25 × fs — exactly InstUI's Heading line-height. Rows stack with no gap: the padding is the leading, carried inside each row rather than between them, so it's present even on a single row. Block height is rows × row-height. xxs is the exception. It stands in for legend, a body style with no Heading equivalent, so it uses the body ratio instead: 3px padding on a 12px bar, for an 18px row. The derivation rule Bar height = the font-size of the text style being replaced. Block height = rows × line-height — Heading uses 1.25 × font-size, Text uses 1.5 × font-size. xxs follows the Text ratio (1.5), not the Heading one — it replaces legend, which has no Heading equivalent. States Skeleton has no interactive states — no hover, focus, or active, since it's not clickable or focusable. Loading: Shimmering shapes matching the eventual content's structure. Reduced motion: Same shapes, shimmer disabled, fully static. Loaded: Skeleton is removed and replaced with real content. Empty (handled by the consumer, not Skeleton itself): Real empty-state message and optional action — never leave skeleton shapes waiting for content that isn't coming. Error (handled by the consumer, not Skeleton itself): Real error state (what failed, plus retry), announced via role="alert". Usage SkeletonLoader provides animated placeholder content that indicates where data will appear while a page or section is loading. ✅ Use SkeletonLoader when • Content is loading asynchronously and you want to show a preview of the expected layout • Replacing a spinner when the page structure is known and worth previewing • Displaying placeholder rows in a list, table, or feed while data is being fetched • Loading user profiles or media where circular and rectangular shapes preview avatars and images 🚫 Don't use SkeletonLoader when • The loading time is very short (under 300ms) — a brief delay without any indicator is less distracting • You need to communicate progress percentage — use a ProgressBar instead • The content has already loaded but is empty — use an EmptyState component instead • An action is processing (e.g. form submission) — use a Spinner or loading button state instead • A user-triggered action is in progress (e.g. clicking Save) — use the Button's busy state instead. Only move focus when the user's own action triggered the load and the result is what they were waiting to interact with — e.g. a "Load more" button, a form submission that reveals a result panel. In that case, move focus to the start of the newly-loaded content, not to the removed skeleton's former position. Layout & colour Skeleton dimensions must approximate the final content closely enough to prevent layout shift — a skeleton shorter than its content pushes the page down when data lands, which is the thing skeletons exist to prevent. Loading is never signalled by shape or colour alone; the role="status" announcement is the accessibility guarantee. implementation: Pure CSS shimmer, no client-JS dependency — behaviour must be identical pre- and post-hydration. Compose from the shared primitives (Skeleton.Text, Skeleton.Avatar, Skeleton.Image) rather than one-off markup per feature. The shimmer is purely decorative — the shape and the region-level announcement carry all the necessary information, so nothing is lost when it is disabled. Per WCAG 2.2.2, cap the loop at or under 5 seconds — roughly 3 cycles (~4.5s) — after which the shape holds static. Longer than that requires a pause/stop/hide control, which doesn't exist here and would be excessive for a decorative shape. "Stops when content arrives" is not sufficient on its own: a hung request would otherwise shimmer indefinitely. The distinction that matters most: Skeleton means content is loading, and this is approximately what it will look like. Loading state more broadly means an operation is happening. Those are different problems with different solutions — conflating them is the single most common Skeleton misuse. Skeleton previews content; everything else in this table communicates that something is being processed. When to use a loading state Use one whenever the user would otherwise stare at a blank or frozen UI while something asynchronous resolves. Exception: if an operation reliably resolves in well under ~200–300ms, skip it entirely — flashing an indicator for 100ms and then swapping to content reads as slower, not faster. If a request is sometimes fast and sometimes slow, delay showing any indicator by 200–500ms so fast responses never show one.
